title: Batman (TV series)
wiki_lead:
Batman is an American superhero comedy television series created by William Dozier based on the DC Comics character of the same name that aired on ABC for three seasons and 120 episodes from January 12, 1966, to March 14, 1968.
It stars Adam West as Bruce Wayne/Batman and Burt Ward as Dick Grayson/Robin—two crime-fighting heroes who defend Gotham City from a variety of archvillains.
Known for its camp style and upbeat theme music, as well as its intentionally humorous, simplistic morality aimed at its preteen audience, the show aired twice weekly during the first two seasons, and weekly for the third. A companion feature film was released in 1966 between the first and second seasons of the show.
Batman had the most episodes of a superhero television series (120 episodes) until it was surpassed by Smallville in 2007 (217 episodes).

Overview
The series centers on "millionaire playboy" Bruce Wayne and his "youthful ward" Dick Grayson who, in the guise of their alter-egos Batman and Robin, defend Gotham City from various arch-criminals. Although the lives of their true identities are frequently shown, it is usually only briefly, in the context of their being called away on superhero business or in circumstances where they need to employ their actual identities to assist in their crime-fighting. The "Dynamic Duo" typically comes to the aid of the Gotham City Police Department upon the latter being stumped by a supervillain, who is usually accompanied in their appearances by several henchmen, often with nicknames themed around the criminal or the crime, and, in the case of male villains, an attractive female companion. Throughout each episode, Batman and Robin follow a series of seemingly improbable clues (also known as "bat logic") to discover the supervillain's plan, then figure out how to thwart that plan and capture the criminal.
For the first two seasons, Batman was broadcast twice a week, on consecutive nights. Every story is in two parts, except for two three-parters featuring villainous team-ups (the Joker and the Penguin, then the Penguin and Marsha, Queen of Diamonds) in the second season. The titles of each multi-part story usually rhyme. The third and final season, which aired one episode a week and introduced Yvonne Craig as Barbara Gordon/Batgirl, consists of self-contained stories. Each third-season story ends with a teaser featuring the next episode's guest villain, except for the series finale. The cliffhangers between multiple-part stories consist of villains holding someone captive, usually Batman and/or Robin, with the captive(s) being threatened by death, serious injury, or another fate. These cliffhangers are resolved early in follow-up episodes, with captives escaping the traps.
Ostensibly a crime series, the show's style is intentionally campy and tongue-in-cheek. It exaggerates serious and tense circumstances, playing them for laughs, while the characters take the ludicrous situations very seriously.

grok_lead: Batman is an American live-action television series based on the DC Comics character, starring Adam West as Bruce Wayne / Batman and Burt Ward as Dick Grayson / Robin, which aired on ABC from January 12, 1966, to March 14, 1968. The program, produced by William Dozier for Greenway Productions and Twentieth Century-Fox Television, consists of 120 episodes across three seasons, featuring the Dynamic Duo combating Gotham City's colorful villains using gadgets, moral lessons, and signature onomatopoeic sound effects like "Pow!" and "Bam!" in a deliberately exaggerated, campy style intended to satirize superhero tropes while appealing to children and families. Initially a ratings phenomenon, the series drew an average of 14.5 million viewers per episode in its first season, ranking in the top five programs and sparking "Batmania" with over $75 million in merchandise sales in 1966 alone, alongside Emmy nominations for sound editing and comedy series. However, viewership declined sharply by the third season due to rising production costs, repetitive formulas, and audience fatigue, leading to cancellation midway through, which some critics argued perpetuated a comical perception of Batman that overshadowed the character's darker comic origins for years.
